categories.label: God, Faith + Doubt
categories.description: Questions about whether Christianity is true, whether God can be trusted, and what to do with honest doubt.

categories.label: Suffering, Evil + Justice
categories.description: Questions about pain, injustice, unanswered prayer, and the tension between a good God and a broken world.

categories.label: Identity, Purpose + Self
categories.description: Questions about worth, calling, freedom, happiness, ambition, and what makes a life meaningful.

categories.label: Relationships, Sex + Family
categories.description: Questions about love, marriage, singleness, forgiveness, boundaries, sexuality, parenting, and loyalty.

categories.label: Truth, Morality + Culture
categories.description: Questions about moral truth, tolerance, disagreement, conscience, social pressure, and living faithfully in a pluralistic culture.

categories.label: Work, Money + Ambition
categories.description: Questions about success, career, wealth, generosity, status, contentment, and responsibility.

categories.label: AI, Technology + Human Worth
categories.description: Questions about AI, automation, attention, privacy, companionship, creativity, and what remains distinctively human.

categories.label: Science, Origins + Future
categories.description: Questions about science and faith, origins, consciousness, medicine, progress, mortality, and humanity's future.

categories.label: Church, Christians + Hypocrisy
categories.description: Questions about church hurt, hypocrisy, authority, disagreement, scandals, and whether failures of Christians undermine Christianity.

categories.label: Everyday Wisdom + Decisions
categories.description: Questions about knowing what is wise when there is no obvious rule, certainty, or perfect option.

topics.title: Why should I believe Christianity is true, not merely comforting?
topics.summary: Separate emotional usefulness from whether the central claims of Christianity are actually true.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: You are open to Christianity but worry that belief may simply meet a psychological need.
topics.stakeholder: the person trying to distinguish hope from wishful thinking
topics.risk: comfort being mistaken for evidence
topics.badIncentive: comfort being mistaken for evidence
topics.wiseLimit: test the claim using reason, history, coherence, and lived consequences

topics.title: Why does God seem hidden from sincere people?
topics.summary: Explore why a God who wants to be known may still not make His presence undeniable.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Someone sincerely asks for God to reveal Himself and experiences silence.
topics.stakeholder: the sincere seeker who feels ignored
topics.risk: silence being treated as proof of absence
topics.badIncentive: silence being treated as proof of absence
topics.wiseLimit: distinguish hiddenness, freedom, evidence, expectation, and the kind of relationship being sought

topics.title: Can genuine faith include serious doubt?
topics.summary: Ask whether uncertainty destroys faith or can become part of honest intellectual and spiritual growth.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A believer is troubled by questions they cannot resolve and fears that asking them is disloyal.
topics.stakeholder: the person afraid that questions make them faithless
topics.risk: pretending certainty instead of pursuing truth
topics.badIncentive: pretending certainty instead of pursuing truth
topics.wiseLimit: treat doubt as something to examine honestly rather than celebrate or suppress

topics.title: If God already knows what I will choose, am I really free?
topics.summary: Examine whether divine foreknowledge and meaningful human choice logically contradict one another.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: You wonder whether a future already known by God can still contain genuine choices.
topics.stakeholder: the person trying to understand moral responsibility
topics.risk: confusing knowledge of a choice with causing the choice
topics.badIncentive: confusing knowledge of a choice with causing the choice
topics.wiseLimit: define freedom carefully and separate foreknowledge from coercion

topics.title: If God already knows everything, what does prayer actually change?
topics.summary: Explore whether prayer is informing God, changing circumstances, changing the person praying, or participating in providence.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: You wonder why anyone should pray if God already knows every need and outcome.
topics.stakeholder: the person wondering whether prayer has real significance
topics.risk: reducing prayer to information transfer or wish fulfillment
topics.badIncentive: reducing prayer to information transfer or wish fulfillment
topics.wiseLimit: consider relationship, dependence, providence, petition, and formation together

topics.title: Why should the Bible have authority over my own conscience?
topics.summary: Ask what should happen when personal moral intuition conflicts with a biblical claim.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Your conscience strongly favors one conclusion while Scripture appears to point elsewhere.
topics.stakeholder: the person trying to act with integrity
topics.risk: treating either private intuition or interpretation as automatically infallible
topics.badIncentive: treating either private intuition or interpretation as automatically infallible
topics.wiseLimit: test interpretation, conscience, context, and the source of moral authority

topics.title: Is believing in miracles intellectually reasonable?
topics.summary: Examine whether miracles should be rejected in principle or evaluated as historical claims.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A friend says educated people should rule out miracles before looking at the evidence.
topics.stakeholder: the person deciding what evidence is allowed to count
topics.risk: assuming naturalism before the argument begins
topics.badIncentive: assuming naturalism before the argument begins
topics.wiseLimit: distinguish methodological science from a philosophical claim that nature is all that exists

topics.title: What would count as evidence that my belief is wrong?
topics.summary: Test whether faith is open to evidence or protected from every possible challenge.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: You realize you can list reasons for belief but are unsure what could ever make you reconsider.
topics.stakeholder: the believer who wants convictions rather than self-protection
topics.risk: making a worldview impossible to question
topics.badIncentive: making a worldview impossible to question
topics.wiseLimit: identify core claims, evidence, defeaters, and what genuine openness to correction looks like

topics.title: If God is good, why does He allow children to suffer?
topics.summary: Face the strongest emotional and moral form of the problem of evil without offering a shallow explanation.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A child suffers from a disease or violence they did not choose.
topics.stakeholder: the child and family living through undeserved pain
topics.risk: easy answers that minimize real suffering
topics.badIncentive: easy answers that minimize real suffering
topics.wiseLimit: distinguish what can be explained, what remains mysterious, and what the Christian worldview claims God does about evil

topics.title: Why would a good God allow earthquakes, disease, and disasters?
topics.summary: Explore suffering that cannot be traced directly to an individual human choice.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A natural disaster destroys homes and lives indiscriminately.
topics.stakeholder: the person harmed by forces outside human control
topics.risk: using free will as an answer to every kind of suffering
topics.badIncentive: using free will as an answer to every kind of suffering
topics.wiseLimit: consider creation, regular natural order, human finitude, brokenness, and limits of explanation

topics.title: Why does God sometimes seem not to answer desperate prayer?
topics.summary: Ask what unanswered prayer means and what it does not prove about God, faith, or the person praying.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A family prays urgently for healing and the outcome is not what they asked for.
topics.stakeholder: the person who prayed sincerely and is grieving
topics.risk: blaming the sufferer for insufficient faith
topics.badIncentive: blaming the sufferer for insufficient faith
topics.wiseLimit: separate promise, desire, providence, mystery, and false expectations

topics.title: Does the existence of evil make belief in God irrational?
topics.summary: Examine both the force of the objection and the moral assumptions required to call something objectively evil.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Someone argues that terrible evil is incompatible with an all-good, all-powerful God.
topics.stakeholder: the skeptic who sees suffering as decisive evidence
topics.risk: answering a serious argument with slogans
topics.badIncentive: answering a serious argument with slogans
topics.wiseLimit: state the logical and evidential problem clearly and test both theism and alternatives

topics.title: Does forgiveness let people escape justice?
topics.summary: Clarify whether forgiveness means denying harm, cancelling consequences, restoring trust, or surrendering revenge.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Someone who caused serious harm asks to be forgiven but has not repaired what they did.
topics.stakeholder: the person who was harmed
topics.risk: confusing forgiveness with trust or lack of accountability
topics.badIncentive: confusing forgiveness with trust or lack of accountability
topics.wiseLimit: keep mercy, truth, consequences, reconciliation, and safety distinct

topics.title: Why do cruel or dishonest people sometimes prosper?
topics.summary: Ask whether short-term success tells us anything reliable about goodness, justice, or ultimate flourishing.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A dishonest person gains status and wealth while someone acting with integrity loses out.
topics.stakeholder: the person tempted to believe integrity is pointless
topics.risk: equating visible success with moral vindication
topics.badIncentive: equating visible success with moral vindication
topics.wiseLimit: compare short-term outcomes, character, consequences, and the Christian claim about final justice

topics.title: Can suffering have meaning without calling the suffering itself good?
topics.summary: Explore how growth or redemption can emerge from pain without romanticizing the pain.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Someone says their suffering changed them for the better, but they would never call what happened good.
topics.stakeholder: the survivor trying to make sense of what happened
topics.risk: turning tragedy into a sentimental lesson
topics.badIncentive: turning tragedy into a sentimental lesson
topics.wiseLimit: distinguish evil from what can be brought out of evil

topics.title: How could eternal judgment be compatible with a loving God?
topics.summary: Examine the Christian claims about judgment, human freedom, justice, mercy, and the seriousness of rejecting God.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: You struggle to reconcile divine love with the idea of final judgment.
topics.stakeholder: the person who sees judgment as morally disproportionate
topics.risk: using caricatures instead of defining the doctrine being questioned
topics.badIncentive: using caricatures instead of defining the doctrine being questioned
topics.wiseLimit: clarify what Scripture actually claims before weighing justice, mercy, freedom, and consequence

topics.title: What makes a human life valuable if achievement disappears?
topics.summary: Ask whether worth rests on productivity, intelligence, beauty, usefulness, autonomy, or something deeper.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Someone loses a career, ability, status, or independence and wonders what remains of their value.
topics.stakeholder: the person who can no longer prove their worth through performance
topics.risk: making dignity depend on usefulness
topics.badIncentive: making dignity depend on usefulness
topics.wiseLimit: ground dignity in what a human being is rather than what they can produce

topics.title: How do I know my purpose if I never receive a clear sign from God?
topics.summary: Explore vocation and purpose without expecting a personalized supernatural instruction for every major choice.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: You have several reasonable paths and no unmistakable sign telling you which one to take.
topics.stakeholder: the person frozen by fear of choosing outside God's will
topics.risk: treating uncertainty as disobedience
topics.badIncentive: treating uncertainty as disobedience
topics.wiseLimit: use character, wisdom, responsibility, counsel, gifts, circumstances, and freedom under moral boundaries

topics.title: Is happiness supposed to be the goal of life?
topics.summary: Ask whether pursuing happiness directly produces a good life or whether deeper goods should govern it.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A decision promises immediate happiness but conflicts with commitments and character.
topics.stakeholder: the person deciding what deserves to direct a life
topics.risk: making feeling good the highest moral authority
topics.badIncentive: making feeling good the highest moral authority
topics.wiseLimit: distinguish happiness, joy, pleasure, flourishing, and faithfulness

topics.title: Should I always be true to myself?
topics.summary: Examine whether authenticity is enough when desires conflict with truth, duty, or the good of others.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: You feel a strong desire that seems central to who you are but may conflict with a moral commitment.
topics.stakeholder: the person afraid that restraint means living falsely
topics.risk: assuming every deep desire deserves obedience
topics.badIncentive: assuming every deep desire deserves obedience
topics.wiseLimit: ask which self, desires, and loyalties should be trusted and formed

topics.title: Can I be ambitious without making success an idol?
topics.summary: Explore healthy excellence, stewardship, recognition, status, and the point where ambition begins to own a person.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: You want to achieve something difficult and meaningful but notice how much recognition matters to you.
topics.stakeholder: the person trying to pursue excellence without being ruled by status
topics.risk: calling all ambition selfish or all success good
topics.badIncentive: calling all ambition selfish or all success good
topics.wiseLimit: test motive, means, identity, sacrifice, and what happens if recognition never comes

topics.title: Why is comparison so powerful even when I know it is unhealthy?
topics.summary: Examine what envy reveals about identity, gratitude, status, and the standards used to measure a life.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Someone else's success makes your own life feel smaller even though nothing objectively changed.
topics.stakeholder: the person whose peace depends on another person's scoreboard
topics.risk: using gratitude as a slogan without examining desire
topics.badIncentive: using gratitude as a slogan without examining desire
topics.wiseLimit: identify the good being desired and whether comparison has become a source of identity

topics.title: What does failure say about who I am?
topics.summary: Separate a failed attempt, moral failure, and personal worth so accountability does not become self-condemnation.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A major project, relationship, or goal fails and you begin describing yourself as a failure.
topics.stakeholder: the person whose identity collapsed with an outcome
topics.risk: confusing an event with a permanent identity
topics.badIncentive: confusing an event with a permanent identity
topics.wiseLimit: name responsibility honestly while refusing to make performance the source of worth

topics.title: Is freedom doing what I want, or becoming able to want what is good?
topics.summary: Compare freedom as absence of restraint with freedom as the capacity to live according to truth and the good.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A desire feels liberating in the moment but repeatedly leaves you less able to choose otherwise.
topics.stakeholder: the person who wants genuine agency rather than new forms of dependence
topics.risk: defining freedom only as permission
topics.badIncentive: defining freedom only as permission
topics.wiseLimit: test whether a choice enlarges or narrows the capacity for truth, love, responsibility, and self-control

topics.title: Can I forgive someone without trusting them again?
topics.summary: Clarify forgiveness, reconciliation, trust, consequences, and safety when a relationship has been damaged.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Someone apologizes after repeated betrayal and expects the relationship to return immediately to normal.
topics.stakeholder: the person deciding whether renewed access is wise
topics.risk: using forgiveness to pressure someone into unsafe closeness
topics.badIncentive: using forgiveness to pressure someone into unsafe closeness
topics.wiseLimit: separate release of vengeance from restoration of earned trust

topics.title: Can you genuinely love someone while strongly disagreeing with their choices?
topics.summary: Explore whether love requires approval and whether disagreement can remain truthful without becoming contempt.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A close friend makes a major choice you believe is wrong and asks whether you still accept them.
topics.stakeholder: the person who fears that disagreement means rejection
topics.risk: choosing between dishonest affirmation and dehumanizing condemnation
topics.badIncentive: choosing between dishonest affirmation and dehumanizing condemnation
topics.wiseLimit: hold dignity, honesty, patience, boundaries, and relationship together

topics.title: What should hold a marriage together when feelings change?
topics.summary: Ask whether covenant, affection, duty, safety, friendship, and growth have different roles in marriage.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A couple still respects one another but no longer feels the intensity they once did.
topics.stakeholder: the spouse wondering whether lost feelings mean the relationship is over
topics.risk: treating emotion as either irrelevant or absolute
topics.badIncentive: treating emotion as either irrelevant or absolute
topics.wiseLimit: distinguish ordinary seasons from abuse, betrayal, neglect, and repairable distance

topics.title: Does being single mean something is missing from a full life?
topics.summary: Challenge the assumption that romantic partnership is required for adulthood, worth, intimacy, or purpose.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A single adult feels increasingly defined by what friends and family think they lack.
topics.stakeholder: the person whose life is treated as incomplete
topics.risk: making marriage either an idol or an inferior calling
topics.badIncentive: making marriage either an idol or an inferior calling
topics.wiseLimit: consider belonging, friendship, service, desire, grief, and human completeness

topics.title: Why should sex be connected to covenant rather than just consent and love?
topics.summary: Examine whether consent alone captures the meaning, vulnerability, consequences, and promises involved in sex.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Two adults care about one another and see no need for a permanent commitment before becoming sexually involved.
topics.stakeholder: the people whose bodies and futures carry the consequences
topics.risk: reducing sexual ethics to private preference or mere prohibition
topics.badIncentive: reducing sexual ethics to private preference or mere prohibition
topics.wiseLimit: ask what sex communicates and what kind of commitment can truthfully carry that meaning

topics.title: Where is the line between guiding a child and controlling them?
topics.summary: Explore authority, protection, formation, independence, and how responsibility should change as a child matures.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A parent fears that loosening control will expose a teenager to harmful choices.
topics.stakeholder: the child learning responsibility and the parent accountable for care
topics.risk: using either fear or autonomy as the only principle
topics.badIncentive: using either fear or autonomy as the only principle
topics.wiseLimit: match authority to maturity while protecting relationship, truth, and responsibility

topics.title: Does loyalty to family ever require keeping a harmful secret?
topics.summary: Test whether loyalty means protecting people from truth or seeking their real good even when disclosure is costly.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A family asks you to keep silent about behavior that is harming someone else.
topics.stakeholder: the person exposed to harm by the secret
topics.risk: calling concealment love or betrayal truth
topics.badIncentive: calling concealment love or betrayal truth
topics.wiseLimit: weigh confidentiality, safety, justice, repentance, and proper authority

topics.title: Are boundaries selfish, or can they be an expression of love?
topics.summary: Distinguish healthy limits from avoidance, retaliation, indifference, and the belief that love requires endless access.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Someone repeatedly demands time, money, or emotional energy and calls every limit unloving.
topics.stakeholder: the person carrying responsibilities they cannot sustain
topics.risk: using guilt to erase legitimate limits
topics.badIncentive: using guilt to erase legitimate limits
topics.wiseLimit: ask what love actually requires for both people rather than what keeps conflict away

topics.title: Can objective morality exist without God?
topics.summary: Ask what makes moral obligations objectively binding rather than strong personal or social preferences.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Two people agree that cruelty is wrong but disagree about whether that wrongness exists beyond human opinion.
topics.stakeholder: the person asking what moral language ultimately refers to
topics.risk: assuming agreement automatically explains moral authority
topics.badIncentive: assuming agreement automatically explains moral authority
topics.wiseLimit: compare competing accounts of moral facts, duties, human dignity, and accountability

topics.title: Is saying 'that's true for you' ever enough?
topics.summary: Examine the difference between preferences, perspectives, interpretations, and claims about reality.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Two people hold contradictory beliefs and avoid conflict by saying both are true for each person.
topics.stakeholder: the person who still has to act in one shared reality
topics.risk: confusing respect for people with treating contradictions as equally true
topics.badIncentive: confusing respect for people with treating contradictions as equally true
topics.wiseLimit: separate subjective experience from claims that can be true or false

topics.title: Does tolerance require affirming beliefs I think are wrong?
topics.summary: Clarify how a pluralistic society can protect people while permitting serious moral and religious disagreement.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A disagreement becomes framed as proof that one person is hateful or intolerant.
topics.stakeholder: the person trying to remain respectful without pretending agreement
topics.risk: defining tolerance as mandatory approval
topics.badIncentive: defining tolerance as mandatory approval
topics.wiseLimit: protect dignity and civil freedom while allowing truthful disagreement

topics.title: Can my conscience be sincere and still be wrong?
topics.summary: Ask how conscience should be formed, tested, and corrected rather than simply obeyed as an inner authority.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: You feel deeply certain about a moral issue but discover thoughtful people who reach the opposite conclusion.
topics.stakeholder: the person trying to act honestly without making sincerity infallible
topics.risk: equating intensity of conviction with truth
topics.badIncentive: equating intensity of conviction with truth
topics.wiseLimit: test conscience against truth, reasons, consequences, community, and Scripture

topics.title: When does offensive speech become genuine harm?
topics.summary: Distinguish hurt, insult, social pressure, deception, threats, and concrete harms without trivializing any of them.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A public discussion includes views some people experience as deeply offensive.
topics.stakeholder: the people affected by both speech and restrictions on speech
topics.risk: calling every discomfort harm or every speech consequence censorship
topics.badIncentive: calling every discomfort harm or every speech consequence censorship
topics.wiseLimit: define the kind of harm at issue before deciding what response is justified

topics.title: If most people accept something, does that make it morally right?
topics.summary: Explore what social agreement can establish and what it cannot establish about moral truth.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A once-controversial practice becomes widely accepted and dissent becomes socially costly.
topics.stakeholder: the person deciding whether consensus should settle conscience
topics.risk: treating popularity as proof of moral progress or decline
topics.badIncentive: treating popularity as proof of moral progress or decline
topics.wiseLimit: evaluate the reasons beneath consensus rather than the headcount alone

topics.title: Can compassion become harmful when it avoids difficult truth?
topics.summary: Ask whether compassion is simply reducing immediate distress or seeking a person's deeper good.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Telling the truth may cause pain now, while avoiding it may allow a serious problem to continue.
topics.stakeholder: the person who needs both dignity and reality
topics.risk: using kindness to avoid courage or truth to excuse cruelty
topics.badIncentive: using kindness to avoid courage or truth to excuse cruelty
topics.wiseLimit: join truthful diagnosis with proportionate care

topics.title: How do we know whether society is making moral progress?
topics.summary: Ask what standard lets us call one moral era better than another instead of merely different.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A culture celebrates changing norms as progress while critics call them decline.
topics.stakeholder: the person trying to judge change by more than nostalgia or fashion
topics.risk: assuming newer means better or older means wiser
topics.badIncentive: assuming newer means better or older means wiser
topics.wiseLimit: name the moral standard before measuring movement toward or away from it

topics.title: How much success is enough?
topics.summary: Examine what happens when achievement has no natural stopping point and identity depends on the next milestone.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Each promotion or financial goal quickly becomes the baseline for another one.
topics.stakeholder: the person whose life is always postponed until the next achievement
topics.risk: letting comparison define enough
topics.badIncentive: letting comparison define enough
topics.wiseLimit: set success beneath calling, relationships, character, stewardship, and limits

topics.title: Is becoming wealthy morally wrong?
topics.summary: Distinguish possession of wealth from greed, exploitation, stewardship, generosity, and the power wealth creates.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A person builds a profitable business and wonders whether accumulating significant wealth is itself spiritually suspect.
topics.stakeholder: workers, customers, family, and neighbors affected by how wealth is gained and used
topics.risk: treating wealth as either proof of blessing or proof of corruption
topics.badIncentive: treating wealth as either proof of blessing or proof of corruption
topics.wiseLimit: evaluate means, loyalties, generosity, justice, and what money is allowed to command

topics.title: When does career ambition become unfair to family?
topics.summary: Ask how to weigh meaningful work against promises, presence, provision, and responsibilities that cannot be outsourced.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A major career opportunity requires years of heavier travel and less time at home.
topics.stakeholder: family members who absorb the hidden cost of the opportunity
topics.risk: calling every sacrifice necessary because the goal is good
topics.badIncentive: calling every sacrifice necessary because the goal is good
topics.wiseLimit: count costs borne by others, not only benefits received by the decision-maker

topics.title: Should I stay in a job I hate if people depend on me?
topics.summary: Balance provision, mental strain, calling, prudence, and the difference between enduring difficulty and accepting needless damage.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: A job is draining and discouraging, but leaving would create financial risk for the household.
topics.stakeholder: the person carrying both work strain and family responsibility
topics.risk: romanticizing either escape or endurance
topics.badIncentive: romanticizing either escape or endurance
topics.wiseLimit: seek a responsible transition rather than framing the choice as instant departure or permanent resignation

topics.title: How generous should I be when I am also trying to build financial security?
topics.summary: Explore whether prudent saving and sacrificial generosity compete or can be ordered together.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: You have limited margin and several legitimate future responsibilities, but also see immediate needs around you.
topics.stakeholder: people who depend on your provision and people in genuine need
topics.risk: using future fear to justify never giving or guilt to ignore real obligations
topics.badIncentive: using future fear to justify never giving or guilt to ignore real obligations
topics.wiseLimit: define enough, responsibility, sacrifice, and generosity in the same budget

topics.title: Am I responsible for what my employer does?
topics.summary: Ask how much moral responsibility an employee bears for policies, products, or practices they do not fully control.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
topics.scenario: Your role is ordinary, but the organization profits from something you increasingly believe is harmful.
topics.stakeholder: people affected by the organization's conduct and the employee with limited power
topics.risk: pretending employment creates either zero responsibility or total responsibility
topics.badIncentive: pretending employment creates either zero responsibility or total responsibility
topics.wiseLimit: consider proximity, participation, influence, alternatives, and material cooperation

topics.title: Does my work have to feel meaningful to be worthwhile?
topics.summary: Challenge the idea that vocation must always produce passion, prestige, or obvious social impact.
topics.hook: Professor L will help separate the strongest version of the question from assumptions that may be hiding inside it.
